title: Identifying Mediocre People in the Recruiting Process
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece argues for a specific prior in hiring: assume by default that the person across the table is average, because the Mediocrity Principle says a randomly drawn candidate most likely belongs to the most numerous category. Having set that up, it is honest about the difficulty, conceding there is no foolproof way to separate the middle of the distribution from the tail, that track record and pedigree are moderated by too many other factors to support causal claims, and that many people interview better than they work. Its proposed instrument is social rather than analytical: put candidates in front of the high achievers already on the team, on the stated premise that mediocre people dislike high achievers and high achievers detest mediocre people, so honest conversation alone will repel a weak candidate. The essay adds a second benefit, that talent attracts talent and the same exposure helps land candidates worth having. It is careful to bound the claim, presenting this as one component rather than the centrepiece of a recruiting process, and treats the discomfort involved as the price of hiring well.
points: The recommended prior is explicit and defensible: presume you are interviewing an average candidate, because the base rate says the most numerous category is the likeliest draw.
The piece is unusually honest about the limits of the usual signals, noting that track record and pedigree are too heavily moderated to support causal inference about future performance.
The instrument proposed is social rather than analytical, exposing candidates to the team's strongest performers and letting mutual antipathy do the screening.
The same exposure is claimed to work in both directions, repelling mediocre candidates while attracting strong ones, which makes it a recruiting tool as much as a filter.
The scope is deliberately bounded, presented as a component of a process rather than its centrepiece, with the discomfort framed as the price of selecting well.
quotes: That’s why savvy leaders know it is always safer to presume one is interviewing a mediocre talent and not a person of extraordinary skill or ambition.

The Mediocrity Principle suggests that if a person is drawn at random from a population of people with diverse skills and talents, that person is more likely to represent the most numerous category, which is always average or mediocre.
Worse yet, many people are more skilled at interviewing for a role than they are at the work and passion required to do it.
Here is a commonly held fact in any game of excellence: Mediocre people don’t like high achievers and high achievers detest mediocre people.
Designing a talent selection process where the team’s best performers get a crack at assessing those they will work with pays big dividends in the hunt for exceptional talent.
The most ambitious, driven, and skillful team members will repel a mediocre candidate by just engaging in honest conversation.
Better yet, talent always attracts talent, so this exposure makes it easier to reel in candidates worth selecting.
